title: Existential threats join bubble fears as AI mood sobers
author: B
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

Artificial intelligence’s promise faced tougher scrutiny at two Singapore conferences on October 7, as investors and policymakers weighed financial excess alongside potentially catastrophic safety risks.

According to Reuters, discussions at the Milken Institute Asia Summit and Forbes Global CEO Conference broadened beyond expensive technology stocks to questions about human control, malicious use and whether enormous AI investments will generate adequate returns.

Singapore Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan warned that claims of complete control over autonomous agents were misplaced. He also highlighted the danger of state and non-state actors using AI to develop weapons.

Biocon founder and chairperson Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw raised concerns about AI assisting the creation of dangerous pathogens. While recognising its benefits, she called for stronger governance and questioned whether industry self-regulation would be sufficient.

Financial warnings were pointed. Temasek chief investment officer Rohit Sipahimalani said safety problems, regulation or disappointing customer returns could undermine the AI investment narrative. Bridgewater founder Ray Dalio described the boom as a bubble and warned that higher interest rates could help trigger its reversal.

The discussion highlights two distinct uncertainties. One concerns what increasingly capable systems might do; the other concerns how much businesses should pay for their expected benefits. A technology can deliver useful advances while investments built around it still disappoint.

Those uncertainties can also interact. A serious safety incident could damage customer confidence or prompt tighter oversight. Conversely, pressure to justify heavy spending could encourage companies to deploy systems before their limitations are fully understood. These are possible pathways, rather than outcomes established by the conference remarks.

For business leaders, the practical implication is to assess adoption through measurable results and clear accountability. Productivity claims need evidence, while delegated actions need defined boundaries and human review.

The Singapore debate suggests AI’s next phase will demand answers about both value and control.
